paragraphs: When a model must serve several objectives or tasks, improving one outcome can come at the expense of another. Pareto optimality describes solutions where no objective can improve without worsening another. However, finding such a solution does not by itself express which tradeoffs a user prefers. This paper develops a framework that combines these two goals.

The framework accommodates multiple forms of preference within a common formulation for multi-objective optimization and multi-task learning. Its aim is to find a solution that both aligns with the stated preference and achieves Pareto optimality. The authors apply it to weighted Chebyshev optimization, a method for exploring the Pareto front, and to an extension designed to help find a model that improves on an existing model in a single run.

Experiments report competitive performance relative to existing methods while demonstrating different ways to specify preferences. The contribution is therefore a more flexible route to selecting desirable tradeoffs, alongside the optimization needed to achieve them.
icml-2022-a-multi-objective-multi-task-l.tldr: A unified optimization framework seeks Pareto-optimal models while accommodating several forms of user preference.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning asks an agent to earn reward while also meeting requirements such as safety or budget limits. These additional objectives often lead to algorithms with machinery beyond ordinary reinforcement learning. This paper connects the problem to reward-free learning, where an agent learns how the environment changes without relying on a particular reward signal.

The connection matters because several objectives can share the same environment dynamics. Knowledge gathered without committing to one reward can therefore support decisions about multiple objectives. The authors propose a general procedure that uses a reward-free reinforcement learning solver to address both constrained learning and approachability problems, adding negligible overhead in the number of samples required.

With existing reward-free solvers, the framework yields sample-complexity guarantees for tabular decision processes that match the best existing results apart from a horizon-dependent factor. It also extends to tabular two-player Markov games and provides a new result with linear function approximation. These findings make reward-free learning a reusable foundation for several constrained decision problems.
icml-2022-a-simple-reward-free-approach-.tldr: A general procedure converts reward-free reinforcement learning solvers into constrained-learning methods with negligible additional sample complexity.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through discrete, sparse signals, offering a way to handle information across space and time efficiently. Much previous work has concentrated on how to train these networks. This paper instead investigates how architectural choices affect both predictive accuracy and the number of spikes a network generates.

The authors examine design choices used in earlier studies and find that they are not especially well suited to spiking networks. They then introduce AutoSNN, a neural architecture search framework that excludes undesirable choices from its search space. Its search criterion considers both accuracy and spike count, so candidate architectures are evaluated on their predictive performance together with their signaling activity.

Across several datasets, including neuromorphic datasets, the resulting architectures outperform hand-designed spiking networks in accuracy and energy efficiency. The stated findings support treating architecture as an important part of efficient spiking computation. AutoSNN makes that design problem explicit by incorporating spike activity into the process that selects the network itself.
icml-2022-autosnn-towards-energy-efficie.tldr: AutoSNN searches for spiking-network architectures using both accuracy and spike count, improving on hand-designed networks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural-network convergence analyses often assume that initial weight vectors are independently drawn from a Gaussian distribution. This paper changes that construction: weights come in independent pairs, with the two vectors inside each pair identical. The authors show that this coupled initialization substantially improves theoretical bounds on the width needed for training two-layer ReLU networks.

The analysis accommodates arbitrary inputs, extending beyond earlier treatment of random inputs. For an under-parameterized network trained with logistic loss, the required neuron count drops from roughly the inverse eighth power of the neural tangent kernel separation margin to its inverse square. For an over-parameterized network trained with squared loss, the dependence on the number of inputs falls from roughly fourth power to second power.

These are improvements in sufficient widths established by convergence analysis, rather than a claim that every practical network needs those widths. The squared-loss result also improves a prior running-time bound. For the under-parameterized setting, the authors establish stronger lower bounds that are best possible under certain assumptions.
icml-2022-bounding-the-width-of-neural-n.tldr: Initializing weights in identical Gaussian pairs yields substantially smaller provable width requirements for two-layer ReLU networks.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to label, with the goal of learning more efficiently than random sampling. This paper asks where those efficiency gains can appear. It studies a particularly favorable setting: well-specified logistic regression with inputs distributed uniformly over a sphere. Upper and lower bounds establish the attainable dependence of expected excess error on sample count.

In this setting, both active learning and random sampling have error that decreases inversely with the number of samples. The lower bound also rules out a uniformly better sample-count dependence for more general settings that include this case. This limits what adaptive selection can promise about the asymptotic rate, even when the underlying prediction problem is relatively simple.

There is still room for meaningful gains in the factors multiplying that rate. The authors show that a variant of uncertainty sampling improves convergence relative to random sampling by a factor tied to the Bayes error. The result provides theoretical support for a previously observed empirical benefit while locating that benefit in constants rather than a better sample-count exponent.
icml-2022-constants-matter-the-performan.tldr: In the studied logistic-regression setting, active learning improves constant factors while sharing random sampling’s inverse-sample error rate.

paragraphs: Visual-control agents must turn images into representations useful for choosing actions. Reusing those representations across control tasks could reduce the amount of training experience required. This paper introduces CtrlFormer, a transformer architecture designed to learn transferable representations while retaining performance on tasks the agent has already learned.

CtrlFormer jointly learns self-attention relationships involving visual tokens and policy tokens across different control tasks. This provides a structure for learning and transferring multitask representations. The authors pair the architecture with a contrastive reinforcement learning training approach intended to make learning efficient when environment interactions are limited.

The reported DMControl results illustrate both transfer and retention. In the Cartpole example, CtrlFormer reaches a state-of-the-art score with 100,000 samples after transfer while maintaining earlier task performance. Recent advanced methods described in the abstract instead obtain zero scores in that transfer setting with the same sample count. The example supports the proposed combination of architecture and training for efficient transfer; it does not establish that forgetting is absent in every possible task sequence.
icml-2022-ctrlformer-learning-transferab.tldr: CtrlFormer combines multitask transformer representations with contrastive reinforcement learning to improve visual-control transfer while preserving prior-task performance.

paragraphs: Community detection uses graph connections to infer which vertices belong to the same underlying group. This paper studies exact recovery of those groups when individual connections must remain private. Its setting is the stochastic block model, where within-community and between-community connection probabilities determine how clearly the groups are separated.

The privacy requirement is edge differential privacy, which concerns individual links in the graph. The authors analyze how the connection probabilities, privacy budget, and computational cost interact. They compare three types of private recovery mechanisms: methods based on stability, methods based on sampling, and methods that perturb the graph.

Stability and sampling mechanisms offer better tradeoffs between the graph’s connection probabilities and the privacy budget, but demand more computation. Graph perturbation has lower computational complexity, yet exact recovery requires its epsilon privacy budget to grow at least logarithmically with the number of vertices. The findings make computational efficiency part of the privacy–recovery tradeoff, rather than treating all private community-detection procedures as interchangeable.
icml-2022-differentially-private-communi.tldr: Private community recovery exposes a tradeoff between computational cost, graph structure, and the privacy budget needed for exact recovery.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that a representation changes in a structured way when its input is transformed. This paper studies that property as a useful bias for reinforcement learning. It seeks representations that respond consistently both to an agent’s actions and to symmetry transformations applied to state–action pairs.

Earlier symmetry-based approaches described in the abstract can incorporate only predefined linear transformations. EqR instead allows nonlinear symmetry transformations to be learned from data. It combines a Lie-algebra-based parameterization of state and action encodings, latent transition models that respect equivariance, and training losses based on symmetry. Together, these components connect the representation’s structure to transformations and transitions relevant to the agent.

The authors demonstrate advantages on Atari games with experience restricted to 100,000 environment interactions. That setting makes learning from limited data central to the evaluation. The reported findings support learning useful symmetry structure rather than requiring every transformation to be specified beforehand, while the demonstrated benefit remains tied to the evaluated data-efficient reinforcement learning setting.
icml-2022-eqr-equivariant-representation.tldr: EqR learns action-consistent representations and nonlinear symmetries from data, showing benefits in Atari learning with limited interactions.

paragraphs: Training a two-layer ReLU network is usually approached as a nonconvex optimization problem. This paper develops algorithms and software around a convex reformulation of training with weight decay. The reformulation uses groups of models associated with portions of the data, with group regularization and polyhedral cone constraints defining their structure.

The authors clarify when a simpler convex model can represent the training problem. With zero regularization, they establish exact equivalence to unconstrained optimization of a convex gated ReLU network. With nonzero regularization, gated ReLU models instead provide approximation bounds that depend on the data. This distinction separates an exact reformulation from a controlled approximation.

To solve these problems, the paper develops an accelerated proximal gradient method and a practical augmented Lagrangian solver. The reported comparisons show faster optimization than standard nonconvex training heuristics such as SGD and better performance than commercial interior-point solvers. Experiments also examine the regularization path and demonstrate image classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10, connecting the theoretical formulations to usable training procedures.
icml-2022-fast-convex-optimization-for-t.tldr: Convex reformulations and specialized solvers make two-layer ReLU training faster in the reported comparisons, with exact or approximate relationships depending on regularization.

paragraphs: A stochastic linear bandit learner must choose actions while learning how their features relate to reward. This paper adds uncertainty about the appropriate model itself. It considers two forms of model selection and asks how much additional regret arises compared with knowing the correct model in advance.

In feature selection, at least one of several candidate feature maps can express the expected reward linearly. In parameter selection, the reward parameter belongs to one of several possibly overlapping balls in parameter space. The learner has only imperfect estimates of those balls’ centers and radii. For each setting, the authors develop a computationally efficient algorithm by reducing the bandit problem to a full-information problem.

Their regret bounds are no worse than the known-model case up to a square-root-logarithmic factor in the number of candidate models. The authors report this as the best dependence on model count then available for these settings. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data support the algorithms’ effectiveness, complementing the theoretical account of the cost of model uncertainty.
icml-2022-feature-and-parameter-selectio.tldr: Efficient linear-bandit algorithms select features or parameter models with only a square-root-logarithmic regret factor in the number of candidates.

paragraphs: Agents trained through self-play can become effective collaborators while relying on conventions unfamiliar to other partners. This creates a gap between coordinating with training partners and coordinating with someone new. The paper addresses that gap by changing how agents learn about conventions, placing this learning in their beliefs about behavior.

The proposed belief-learning approach can maintain beliefs over trajectories produced by policies that were not seen during training. This lets an agent interpret and adapt to unfamiliar conventions at test time. The authors use the belief model in two ways: to support search and to train a best response over a collection of policies.

The paper reports substantial improvements in zero-shot coordination, where cooperation must work with a novel partner without prior joint training. It also shows that the belief-based approach helps explain and interpret subtle agent conventions. The central contribution is a way to represent uncertainty about partners’ behavior that can generalize beyond the policies used to train the belief model.
icml-2022-generalized-beliefs-for-cooper.tldr: Learning beliefs that generalize to unseen policies helps cooperative agents interpret unfamiliar conventions and coordinate with new partners.

paragraphs: Some causal-discovery methods look for predictive relationships that remain stable across changing environments. Invariant causal prediction uses this idea to identify some direct causes of a response. However, when environments change only a few underlying mechanisms, the identified set can be small or empty. This paper broadens the search from direct causes to causal ancestors.

The authors introduce minimal invariance and build invariant ancestry search around it. In the population version, where the relevant distributional information is available, the method returns only ancestors of the response. Its output also contains everything returned by invariant causal prediction. This gives a precise sense in which the method expands the identified set while retaining a causal interpretation.

For observed data, corresponding guarantees are asymptotic and depend on the invariance test having the required asymptotic level and power. They are therefore conditional large-sample guarantees. The paper also develops scalable algorithms and evaluates them on simulated and real data, connecting the ancestry-search formulation to practical procedures.
icml-2022-invariant-ancestry-search-9cfe.tldr: Invariant ancestry search expands invariant causal prediction’s output to a guaranteed set of causal ancestors, with conditional asymptotic guarantees for data.

paragraphs: A stochastic shortest-path learner must reach a goal while controlling accumulated cost in an uncertain environment. This paper studies environments whose transition dynamics have a linear-mixture representation. That structure allows the analysis to depend on the feature dimension rather than treating every possible transition as an unrelated unknown.

The first algorithm uses Hoeffding-style confidence sets to manage uncertainty. When every cost has a positive lower bound, its regret grows with the square root of the number of episodes, alongside factors involving feature dimension, optimal expected cost, and the minimum cost. It also applies when costs can be zero, with a weaker but still sublinear episode dependence of two-thirds power.

A refined algorithm uses Bernstein-style confidence sets and improves dependence on the optimal expected cumulative cost from power one-and-a-half to linear. The authors also prove a regret lower bound. The improved upper bound matches it apart from logarithmic factors and an inverse-square-root minimum-cost factor, making the near-optimality claim explicitly qualified by that remaining gap.
icml-2022-learning-stochastic-shortest-p.tldr: Confidence-based algorithms achieve sublinear regret for linear-mixture shortest-path learning, with a refined bound approaching the proven lower bound.

paragraphs: Model editing changes selected behaviors of an already-trained network, such as correcting an error or updating knowledge. A difficult part is deciding which inputs an edit should affect. Existing editors described in this paper struggle with loosely related inputs and can deteriorate after many edits, suggesting that their ability to represent an edit’s scope is insufficient.

The proposed method, SERAC, stores edits in an explicit memory. A retrieval-augmented counterfactual model learns to reason over that memory and adjust the base model’s predictions when needed. This creates a higher-capacity editing mechanism in which stored changes help determine how the model should answer a particular input.

The authors introduce three challenging editing problems involving question answering, fact-checking, and dialogue generation. Among the evaluated methods, only SERAC achieves high performance across all three, and it consistently outperforms existing editors by a significant margin. These results support explicit edit memory and learned reasoning over edits as a way to improve both the coverage and selectivity of model updates.
icml-2022-memory-based-model-editing-at-.tldr: SERAC stores edits in memory and learns when to apply them, outperforming evaluated editors across three language-model editing problems.

paragraphs: An adversarial attack makes a carefully chosen, imperceptible change to an input to disrupt a model’s prediction. Measuring resistance on training examples leaves a further question: how well does that resistance extend to new examples? This paper studies that generalization question through theoretical bounds on adversarial risk.

The bounds hold with high probability and relate adversarial risk to three ingredients: empirical adversarial risk, the complexity of the prediction class, and the set of perturbations available to the adversary. Including the perturbation set makes the threat model part of the generalization analysis. The framework applies broadly across models, losses, and adversaries.

The authors demonstrate its use for multiclass classification and several prediction families, including linear models and deep neural networks. They also derive optimistic bounds for smooth losses, obtaining fast-rate guarantees for adversarial deep learning that they describe as the first known to them. These results provide tools for analyzing robust generalization, with the stronger rate statements specifically tied to the smooth-loss case.
icml-2022-on-the-generalization-analysis.tldr: The paper bounds adversarial generalization using training risk, model complexity, and allowed perturbations, with fast-rate results for smooth losses.

paragraphs: Inductive transfer learning uses a model trained on a source task to learn a target task from limited data. A common approach initializes the target model with the pretrained weights and fine-tunes them. PAC-Net starts from the observation that over-parameterized models can often be pruned without reducing their source-task accuracy.

Its procedure has three stages: pruning, allocation, and calibration. It identifies weights essential to the source task, then fine-tunes those essential weights on source data. Finally, it adapts to the target task by updating the remaining redundant weights. This assigns different roles to the weights used for retaining source-task capability and those available for target-task adaptation.

Across the paper’s extensive transfer-learning experiments, PAC-Net achieves reported state-of-the-art performance by a large margin. The findings support using pruning to organize the transfer process, beyond its role in reducing a model’s size. The motivation depends on the availability of redundant capacity, which the abstract describes as a frequent property of over-parameterized models rather than a universal guarantee.
icml-2022-pac-net-a-model-pruning-approa.tldr: PAC-Net uses pruning to separate source-essential weights from redundant weights that can be adapted to a target task.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent introduces noise through its updates, and that noise influences how training leaves local minima. For mean-square loss, the noise has a multiplicative structure that complicates analysis. This paper uses a random change of time to obtain a stochastic differential equation with a simpler additive-noise description.

Within that formalism, the escape rate depends on the logarithm of the ratio between the loss at a saddle and the loss at a local minimum. This differs from earlier physics-inspired results based on the difference between those two loss values. The distinction makes the relative height of the barrier central to the escape-rate formula.

The formula also depends strongly on the typical magnitude and number of outlying eigenvalues of the Hessian, which characterizes local curvature. The authors use this dependence to explain the empirical tendency of SGD to favor flat minima with low effective dimension. The result offers an account of SGD’s implicit preferences through its noise and local loss geometry in the analyzed mean-square-loss setting.
icml-2022-power-law-escape-rate-of-sgd-b.tldr: An analysis of SGD noise links escape from minima to logarithmic loss barriers and curvature, explaining preferences for flat, low-dimensional minima.

paragraphs: Training on large datasets can waste computation on examples that are already mastered or too noisy to learn usefully. Selecting difficult examples alone does not solve this problem, because high loss can reflect noise or low relevance. Selecting easy examples also has a weakness: they may no longer contribute once the model has learned them.

RHO-LOSS prioritizes examples according to how much they are expected to reduce generalization loss. Its selection approximates a preference for examples that the model can learn, that matter for the task, and that it has not yet mastered. This connects training-data selection to improvement beyond the selected training examples themselves.

The authors report fewer training steps, improved accuracy, and faster training across multiple datasets, hyperparameters, and model families, including MLPs, CNNs, and BERT. On Clothing-1M, the method uses 18 times fewer steps and reaches 2% higher final accuracy than uniform data shuffling. That example quantifies the reported benefit in training steps; it should not be read as an identical multiplier for elapsed training time.
icml-2022-prioritized-training-on-points.tldr: RHO-LOSS accelerates training by prioritizing examples estimated to improve generalization that are learnable and not yet mastered.

paragraphs: Random reshuffling processes a finite collection of training objectives without replacement. This paper extends it to objectives that combine an average of smooth terms with a convex regularizer that may be nonsmooth. Its first algorithm, ProxRR, applies the proximal operation associated with the regularizer only once per epoch.

Reducing how often that operation runs matters when it is expensive. Compared with methods that perform it at every iteration, ProxRR can be up to n times faster for an objective containing n smooth terms. The gain is conditional on the cost of the proximal operation. In distributed optimization, that operation can correspond to communication across the network.

The authors derive FedRR as a federated special case and prove a smaller communication footprint than distributed gradient descent or Local SGD. Their theory covers convex and nonconvex regimes, constant and decreasing step sizes, and importance resampling that can improve conditioning. Experiments on real datasets support the analysis, connecting the reduced frequency of expensive operations to practical optimization benefits.
icml-2022-proximal-and-federated-random-.tldr: ProxRR performs expensive proximal operations once per epoch, and its federated specialization reduces the proven communication footprint.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems combine a smooth objective with a nonsmooth term handled by a proximal operation. Standard proximal gradient descent evaluates both operations every iteration. ProxSkip targets the regime where the proximal operation costs substantially more than a gradient computation, allowing it to be skipped during most iterations.

The stated iteration complexity scales with the condition number times the logarithm of inverse target error. The number of proximal evaluations scales only with the square root of the condition number times that same logarithmic factor. The method therefore improves the count of expensive operations without requiring an equivalent reduction in the total number of iterations.

In federated learning, a gradient step can be computed locally on devices, while the proximal operation corresponds to communication through gradient averaging. ProxSkip’s reduction then becomes a communication-complexity improvement. The authors establish this benefit without assumptions bounding data heterogeneity, addressing a setting where several existing local-gradient methods have theoretical communication costs no better than ordinary gradient descent.
icml-2022-proxskip-yes-local-gradient-st.tldr: ProxSkip provably reduces expensive proximal evaluations, yielding federated communication acceleration without heterogeneity-bounding assumptions.

paragraphs: An ensemble combines several models’ predictions into one decision. Earlier information-theoretic analyses used model accuracy and diversity to lower-bound classification error. This paper argues that those analyses omit an important part of the system: information can be lost when the separate predictions are combined into the final output.

The authors revisit the original form of Fano’s inequality and generalize the earlier theory to include this combination-stage information loss. This expands the basis for evaluating an ensemble beyond the qualities of its individual members and their differences. The way predictions are aggregated becomes part of the theoretical account of the system’s performance.

Experiments on actual ensemble systems empirically validate and illustrate the proposed framework. Its metrics reveal different strengths and weaknesses within a system, offering a more differentiated interpretation than accuracy or diversity alone. The contribution is an evaluation theory that can inform ensemble design by accounting for both the information supplied by component models and what survives their combination.
icml-2022-rethinking-fanos-inequality-in.tldr: An expanded information-theoretic account of ensembles includes information lost when component predictions are combined.

paragraphs: Graph networks should respond consistently when nodes are relabeled, a property called permutation equivariance. Ordinary message-passing networks have limits on the equivariant functions they can approximate. More expressive higher-order alternatives often require large tensors or consideration of every group of k nodes, creating memory costs that grow exponentially with order.

SpeqNets use new heuristics for graph isomorphism to construct a class of universal, permutation-equivariant networks. The architectures adapt to graph sparsity and offer fine-grained control over the balance between expressivity and scalability. This addresses the cost of higher-order modeling by making graph structure relevant to how much computation the network requires.

In supervised node-level and graph-level classification and regression, the authors report substantially shorter computation times than standard higher-order graph networks. They also report significantly better predictive performance than standard graph neural networks and graph kernels. These findings support the architecture family as a practical way to explore richer graph representations while controlling their computational demands.
icml-2022-speqnets-sparsity-aware-permut.tldr: SpeqNets adapt higher-order graph modeling to sparsity, offering adjustable expressivity and scalability with strong reported predictive results.

paragraphs: Maximum-state-entropy exploration encourages an agent to spread its visits across an environment without using rewards. A standard formulation measures the entropy of expected state visitations, and stochastic policies based on the current state are sufficient for that objective. This paper examines what changes when exploration quality is assessed within a single trial.

The revised objective takes the expected entropy of the visitations generated during that trial. Moving the expectation outside the entropy changes the policy requirements. The authors show that deterministic policies allowed to depend on history are sufficient for the revised objective, whereas Markovian policies can incur nonzero regret in general.

The stronger role for history comes with a computational obstacle: finding an optimal history-dependent policy is NP-hard. The paper discusses possible tractable approaches and how such exploration could eventually improve online reinforcement learning’s sample efficiency. Those future benefits are presented as avenues to pursue, while the established results concern policy sufficiency, the limits of Markovian policies, and optimization hardness.
icml-2022-the-importance-of-non-markovia.tldr: For a single-trial entropy objective, history-dependent exploration can outperform Markovian policies, although finding an optimal policy is NP-hard.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learner may need to determine whether contextual information is useful at all. This paper studies that basic model-selection problem: distinguishing a simple multi-armed bandit from a linear contextual bandit. Even this choice can require exploration that differs from what is needed to optimize decisions within a fixed model.

The authors introduce algorithms that adapt exploration to the data and provide model-selection guarantees without feature-diversity conditions. Their bounds take the form of a power of the feature dimension multiplied by a complementary power of the number of rounds. The first algorithm simultaneously recovers two earlier results that were established under different distributional assumptions.

The second algorithm removes distributional assumptions altogether for the studied selection problem, extending where tractable model selection is available. The approach also extends to selection among nested linear contextual models, although that extension needs additional assumptions. Together, the results show how adapting exploration can reduce dependence on restrictive assumptions about the features while retaining formal guarantees for choosing the model.
icml-2022-universal-and-data-adaptive-al.tldr: Data-adaptive exploration enables bandit model selection without feature-diversity conditions, with one algorithm also removing distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: When a neural network learns successive tasks or encounters changing data, new training can damage knowledge acquired earlier. Continual-learning research often addresses this catastrophic forgetting through specialized algorithms. This paper instead investigates the network architecture itself, asking how its width affects the amount of forgetting.

The authors find that width has a substantial effect, with wider networks forgetting less in their empirical study. To understand the result, they examine learning dynamics through gradient orthogonality, sparsity, and the lazy-training regime. These perspectives provide different ways to investigate how updates associated with new learning interact with behavior established earlier.

The proposed explanations are consistent with results across multiple architectures and continual-learning benchmarks. They are presented as potential explanations, rather than as a uniquely established cause of the observed effect. The findings make width a meaningful architectural consideration in continual learning and show that understanding forgetting requires attention to model properties alongside the algorithms used to train models sequentially.
icml-2022-wide-neural-networks-forget-le.tldr: Wider networks show less catastrophic forgetting in the reported experiments, with several learning-dynamics perspectives offering possible explanations.
